lit: the reverse side of the die comes up: the opposite of the face you were hoping for

use.how: Subject is a choice, plan or move that was meant to help: 〜したのが裏目に出た. It turned out to do the opposite of its aim.

near.diff: 水の泡 is effort that comes to nothing; 裏目に出る is a move that produces the opposite of what it aimed at.
墓穴を掘る stresses that one ruined oneself by one's own act, often by talking; 裏目に出る is any well-meant move that backfires.

cue: A shop cut its prices to win customers, but buyers decided the goods must be cheap junk and sales fell. What happened to the plan?

ctx.s: 良[よ]かれと思[おも]って言[い]ったことが{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]た}。

ctx.s: 近道[ちかみち]をしようとしたのが{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]て}、かえって遅[おそ]くなった。
ctx.en: Trying to take a shortcut backfired and I ended up even later.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]の選手[せんしゅ]交代[こうたい]が{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]て}、チームは逆転[ぎゃくてん]負[ま]けした。
ctx.en: The manager's substitution backfired, and the team lost after leading.

ctx.s: 「慎重[しんちょう]すぎたのが{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]た}かな」「うん、もう少[すこ]し早[はや]く決[き]めればよかったね」
ctx.en: "Maybe being so cautious backfired." "Yeah, we should have decided a bit sooner."

ctx.s: 今日[きょう]はやることなすこと{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]る}。

ctx.s: 円安[えんやす]を見越[みこ]した投資[とうし]は、急[きゅう]な円高[えんだか]で{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]た}。
ctx.en: The investment made in expectation of a weaker yen backfired when the yen suddenly strengthened.

bad.en: (meant: the rain caused the match to be cancelled)

lit: a hand reaches out of one's throat to grab the thing one craves

near.diff: 目がない is a lasting weakness for a kind of thing (甘い物に目がない); 喉から手が出る is craving one particular thing right now.

ctx.s: あのゲーム機[き]が{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しい。

ctx.s: 今[いま]、{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しいものってある？

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]が{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しがっていたのは、お金[かね]ではなく自由[じゆう]な時間[じかん]だった。
ctx.en: What he craved more than anything was not money but time of his own.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は甘[あま]いものには{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}。
bad.en: (meant: I have a weakness for sweets)

lit: the food is so good that one's cheeks fall off

ctx.s: 北海道[ほっかいどう]で、{ほっぺたが落[お]ちる}ほどおいしいものを食[た]べたことある？

mean: to refuse to listen to anyone

near.diff: 頭が固い is rigid thinking as a trait; 聞く耳を持たない is shutting out what people are telling one about a matter.

ctx.s: どうしてあの人[ひと]は、医者[いしゃ]の忠告[ちゅうこく]に{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]とうとしない}のだろう。

mean: to add one remark too many and spoil things

口が滑る is letting slip what should stay secret; 一言多い is saying something needless that annoys.

ctx.en: I paid a compliment, then tacked on a 'but', and kicked myself for saying one word too many again.

ctx.s: 上司[じょうし]に謝[あやま]ったのはよかったが、最後[さいご]に言[い]い訳[わけ]をしたのは{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]かった}。
ctx.en: Apologising to the boss was fine, but the excuse at the end was one remark too many.

ctx.s: 「ねえ、私[わたし]って{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]い}かな？」

ctx.s: 夫[おっと]の{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]い}癖[くせ]のせいで、せっかくの雰囲気[ふんいき]が台無[だいな]しになった。

lit: to stick a flaw onto something

near.diff: 揚げ足を取る pounces on slips in someone's words; けちをつける finds petty fault with a thing, plan or result.

mean: to put on a front to look better off than one is
lit: to puff up one's mie, the way one looks in other people's eyes

use.how: Said of someone (often oneself) spending, claiming or acting beyond reality to impress: 見栄を張って高い店でおごる. Mild criticism.

near.diff: 猫をかぶる hides one's real character behind a meek act; 見栄を張る makes oneself look richer or more capable than one is.
鯖を読む fudges a number such as one's age; 見栄を張る is any show of status or ability one does not really have.

ctx.s: 無理[むり]して{見栄[みえ]を張[は]らなくて}もいいよ。

t: 穴があったら入りたい
r: あながあったらはいりたい
mean: so embarrassed one wants to disappear
lit: if there were a hole, I would crawl into it

肩身が狭い is a lasting feeling of being looked down on in a group; 穴があったら入りたい is a burst of embarrassment.

mean: a piece of cake, very easy
lit: before breakfast: so easy it could be done before one has even eaten

near.diff: お安い御用 is a warm 'happy to' in reply to a favour; 朝飯前 describes a task as easy for someone, often boastfully.

mean: no trouble at all, happy to do it
lit: a cheap errand: 'cheap' in the sense that it costs one hardly any effort

near.diff: 朝飯前 says a task is easy for one, often boastfully; お安い御用 is a warm yes to someone's request.

ctx.s: 荷物[にもつ]を預[あず]かるくらい、{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}さ。
ctx.en: Looking after your bags? That's no trouble at all.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]にいいの？忙[いそが]しいんじゃない？」「これくらい{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}だって」
ctx.en: "Are you sure? Aren't you busy?" "Something this small? Happy to do it."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]に電球[でんきゅう]の交換[こうかん]を頼[たの]まれ、「{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}」と笑[わら]って引[ひ]き受[う]けた。
ctx.en: When my grandmother asked me to change a light bulb, I laughed and said, "No trouble at all."

ctx.s: 写真[しゃしん]を頼[たの]まれた男性[だんせい]は「{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}ですよ」とカメラを受[う]け取[と]った。
ctx.en: Asked to take a photo, the man said, "Happy to," and took the camera.

ctx.s: 「遠慮[えんりょ]しないで。駅[えき]まで送[おく]るよ。{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}だ」と叔父[おじ]は車[くるま]の鍵[かぎ]を取[と]った。
ctx.en: "Don't be shy. I'll drive you to the station. Happy to do it," said my uncle, picking up his car keys.

bad.s: この問題[もんだい]は{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}なので、すぐに解[と]けた。
bad.en: (meant: this problem was easy, so I solved it right away)
bad.why: It is a reply agreeing to a favour, not a description of an easy task; for that say asameshimae or kantan.

bad.s: このかばんはセールで{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: this bag was cheap in the sale)
bad.why: Here yasui means 'easy to grant' and has nothing to do with price; for a bargain say yasukatta.
